lessons.title: Masculine and Feminine Nouns
lessons.body: In Arabic, every noun is either masculine or feminine. There is no neutral gender. Most feminine nouns end with the letter Ø© (taa' marbuta), pronounced as 'a' when pausing. For example, 'mu'allima' (female teacher) ends with Ø©, while 'mu'allim' (male teacher) does not. However, some feminine nouns do not have this ending, such as 'umm' (mother) and 'bint' (daughter). You must learn these exceptions. In African markets, knowing gender helps you speak correctly. If you are in Kano, Nigeria, buying fabric, you might say 'hadhihi thobe' (this is a thobe) for a male garment, but 'hadhihi jallabiyya' (this is a jallabiyya) for a female one. Gender also affects adjectives and verbs. For instance, 'kabiir' (big) becomes 'kabiira' for feminine. Practice with everyday items: 'baab' (door) is masculine, 'naafidha' (window) is feminine. In Cairo, Egypt, a taxi driver might say 'al-sayyaara jamiila' (the car is beautiful) â 'sayyaara' is feminine, so the adjective ends with Ø©. In Morocco, 'dar' (house) is feminine, so you say 'dar kabiira' (big house). To master gender, create flashcards with nouns from your environment. Label objects in your home or workplace. For example, in a Nairobi office, label 'kursi' (chair â masculine) and 'taawila' (table â feminine). Listen to Arabic news or songs and note the gender of nouns. Over time, you will internalize the patterns. Remember, mistakes are normal; keep practicing with native speakers in your community. Many African Muslims learn Arabic through Quranic recitation, which reinforces gender rules. For instance, 'al-hamdu lillah' (all praise is due to Allah) uses masculine 'hamd'. By focusing on gender from the start, you build a strong foundation for speaking and writing Arabic accurately.

lessons.title: The Definite Article 'Al-' and Sun/Moon Letters
lessons.body: The Arabic definite article 'al-' means 'the'. It attaches to nouns, like 'al-kitaab' (the book). However, its pronunciation changes depending on the first letter of the noun. Arabic letters are divided into 'sun letters' (al-huruf al-shamsiyya) and 'moon letters' (al-huruf al-qamariyya). With moon letters, you pronounce the 'l' in 'al-'. For example, 'al-qamar' (the moon) â you say the 'l'. With sun letters, the 'l' is not pronounced; instead, the first letter of the noun is doubled. For example, 'al-shams' (the sun) is pronounced 'ash-shams'. The sun letters are: t, th, d, dh, r, z, s, sh, s, d, t, z, l, n. The moon letters are the rest, including a, b, j, h, kh, 'a, gh, f, q, k, m, w, y. In African contexts, this matters for correct speech. In Zanzibar, Tanzania, where Arabic influence is strong, you might hear 'as-salaam alaykum' â the 's' is a sun letter, so 'al-salaam' becomes 'as-salaam'. In Egypt, 'al-nil' (the Nile) â 'n' is a sun letter, so it is pronounced 'an-nil'. Practice by grouping nouns: 'al-bayt' (the house) â moon letter, 'al-shams' (the sun) â sun letter. Use a chart to memorize. Listen to Quranic recitation; you will hear the rules applied perfectly. For example, 'al-rahman' (the Most Merciful) â 'r' is a sun letter, so it is 'ar-rahman'. In daily conversation, saying 'al-shukr' (thanks) becomes 'ash-shukr'. To practice, take a list of common nouns and classify them. Then say them aloud, applying the rule. In a market in Accra, Ghana, if you ask for 'al-fil' (the elephant â moon letter), you pronounce the 'l'. But for 'al-samak' (the fish â sun letter), you say 'as-samak'. This rule is essential for fluency. Write sentences using both types. For instance, 'al-walad fi al-madrasa' (the boy is in the school) â 'w' and 'm' are moon letters, so both 'l's are pronounced. With practice, it becomes automatic. Many learners find it helpful to record themselves and compare with native speakers. Remember, the definite article is used much more in Arabic than in English. So mastering 'al-' is key to speaking naturally.

lessons.title: Indefinite Nouns and Tanwin
lessons.body: In Arabic, indefinite nouns (a/an) are marked by 'tanwin', which is a double vowel at the end of the word. There are three types: 'an' (fatá¸¥atÄn), 'un' (á¸ammatÄn), and 'in' (kasratÄn). For example, 'kitaabun' (a book), 'kitaaban' (a book, in accusative), 'kitaabin' (a book, in genitive). The tanwin is pronounced but not written as a separate letter; it is written as a double vowel sign. In everyday speech, the final 'n' sound is often dropped, but in formal Arabic, it is pronounced. For African learners, tanwin is crucial for reading the Quran and understanding news broadcasts. For instance, in the Quran, 'innallaha ghafurun raheem' â 'ghafurun' and 'raheem' have tanwin. In a market in Khartoum, Sudan, if you want to buy 'a kilo of sugar', you say 'kilo sukkarin' â 'sukkar' (sugar) takes 'in' because it follows a preposition. Tanwin also indicates indefiniteness: 'baytun' (a house) versus 'al-bayt' (the house). When you learn nouns, always learn them with their tanwin. For example, 'waladun' (a boy), 'bintun' (a girl). Practice by making sentences: 'hadha kitaabun' (this is a book). In Egyptian Arabic, tanwin is often dropped in speech, but in formal Arabic, it is essential. To master tanwin, read Arabic texts aloud, paying attention to the endings. Listen to news from Al Jazeera or BBC Arabic; you will hear tanwin clearly. In West Africa, where Arabic is used in Islamic education, students memorize nouns with tanwin. For example, 'madrasatun' (a school), 'mudarrisun' (a teacher). Use flashcards with the tanwin written. Also, note that tanwin is not used with definite nouns or proper nouns. For example, 'Muhammadun' is not used; you say 'Muhammad' without tanwin. Similarly, 'al-kitaabu' has no tanwin. So, when you see a noun without 'al-' and with a double vowel, it is indefinite. Practice writing sentences with indefinite nouns. For instance, 'fi baytin kabiirain' (in a big house) â both 'bayt' and 'kabiir' have tanwin. This may seem complex, but with regular practice, it becomes natural. Use online resources like 'Arabic Verb Trainer' or apps like 'Duolingo' to drill tanwin. In Africa, many madrasas teach tanwin early. So, embrace it as a core part of Arabic grammar.

lessons.title: Singular, Dual, and Plural Forms
lessons.body: Arabic has three numbers: singular (mufrad), dual (muthanna), and plural (jam'). The dual is used for exactly two items, and it is formed by adding 'aani' (for nominative) or 'ayni' (for accusative/genitive) to the singular. For example, 'kitaab' (book) becomes 'kitaabaani' (two books) or 'kitaabayni' (two books, in object position). The plural is more complex. Masculine sound plurals add 'uuna' (nominative) or 'iina' (accusative/genitive). For example, 'mu'allim' (teacher) becomes 'mu'allimuuna' (teachers) or 'mu'allimiina'. Feminine sound plurals add 'aat'. For example, 'mu'allima' (female teacher) becomes 'mu'allimaat'. However, many nouns have broken plurals, which change the internal pattern. For example, 'kitaab' (book) becomes 'kutub' (books). 'walad' (boy) becomes 'awlaad' (boys). 'bint' (girl) becomes 'banaat' (girls). In African contexts, you will use these forms daily. In a classroom in Mali, a teacher might say 'at-tullaab' (the students) â broken plural of 'taalib'. In a shop in Senegal, you might ask for 'kutub' (books). The dual is used for pairs: 'yadaani' (two hands), 'rijlaani' (two feet). In the Quran, you find 'al-samaawaati wa al-ard' (the heavens and the earth) â 'samaawaat' is a feminine plural. To learn plurals, memorize common nouns with their plural forms. Use a notebook: write singular, dual, and plural. For example, 'qalam' (pen) â 'qalamaan' (two pens) â 'aqlaam' (pens). 'sayyaara' (car) â 'sayyaarataan' (two cars) â 'sayyaaraat' (cars). Practice by counting objects around you. In a market in Uganda, count 'tamaatim' (tomatoes) â plural of 'tamaatim'? Actually, 'tamaatim' is plural of 'tamaatima'? Better: 'tamaatim' is plural of 'tamaatim'? Let's use 'tuffaah' (apple) â 'tuffaahataan' (two apples) â 'tuffaahaat' (apples). Listen to native speakers and repeat. Many Arabic dialects simplify dual and plural, but Modern Standard Arabic requires them. For business, knowing plurals helps in negotiations: 'as'aar' (prices) from 'si'r'. In African markets, you might hear 'fuluus' (money) â plural of 'fils'. So, dedicate time to memorizing plural patterns. Use apps like 'Anki' for spaced repetition. With practice, you will recognize patterns and use them correctly.

lessons.title: Demonstratives: This, That, These, Those
lessons.body: Demonstratives in Arabic change based on gender, number, and proximity. For near objects: 'hadha' (this, masculine singular), 'hadhihi' (this, feminine singular), 'haa'ulaa'i' (these, plural for both genders). For far objects: 'dhaalika' (that, masculine singular), 'tilka' (that, feminine singular), 'ulaa'ika' (those, plural). In African Arabic-speaking communities, these are used constantly. For example, in a Cairo market, you might say 'hadha kitaab' (this is a book) or 'hadhihi sayyaara' (this is a car). In Morocco, 'hadha' is often pronounced 'hada' in dialect, but in formal Arabic, it is 'hadha'. To point to something far, 'dhaalika bayt' (that is a house). For plural, 'haa'ulaa'i tullaab' (these are students). Note that demonstratives can be used as pronouns or adjectives. As adjectives, they precede the noun and must agree in gender and number. For example, 'hadha al-walad' (this boy), 'hadhihi al-bint' (this girl). In a shop in Nigeria, you might ask 'bikam hadha?' (how much is this?). The response might be 'dhaalika ghali' (that is expensive). Practice by pointing to objects and saying the correct demonstrative. In a classroom, label items: 'hadha kursi' (this is a chair), 'hadhihi taawila' (this is a table). For far objects, 'dhaalika baab' (that is a door), 'tilka naafidha' (that is a window). For plurals, 'haa'ulaa'i kutub' (these are books), 'ulaa'ika awlaad' (those are boys). Listen to Arabic conversations and note the demonstratives. In the Quran, 'hadha' and 'dhaalika' appear frequently. For example, 'hadha al-Qur'an' (this is the Quran). To master, create sentences with different combinations. In African markets, bargaining often uses 'hadha' and 'dhaalika'. For instance, 'hadha ghali, dhaalika rukhs' (this is expensive, that is cheap). Remember that demonstratives are also used in time expressions: 'hadha al-yawm' (today), 'dhaalika al-yawm' (that day). So, practice with daily situations. Use flashcards with pictures. Watch Arabic cartoons or news and repeat the demonstratives. With consistent practice, you will use them naturally.

lessons.title: Possessive Pronouns and Attached Pronouns
lessons.body: In Arabic, possession is expressed by attaching pronoun suffixes to nouns. These are called 'attached pronouns' (damaa'ir muttasila). For example, 'kitaabi' (my book), 'kitaabuka' (your book, masculine), 'kitaabuki' (your book, feminine), 'kitaabuhu' (his book), 'kitaabuhÄ' (her book), 'kitaabunÄ' (our book), 'kitaabukum' (your book, plural masculine), 'kitaabukunna' (your book, plural feminine), 'kitaabuhum' (their book, masculine), 'kitaabuhunna' (their book, feminine). These suffixes also change the case of the noun. For example, 'kitaabi' is genitive because it is possessed. In African languages, possession is often shown by separate words, but in Arabic, it is attached. This can be challenging, but with practice, it becomes easy. In daily life, you use these constantly. In a family in Somalia, a child might say 'hadha abi' (this is my father) â 'abi' from 'ab' + 'i'. A mother might say 'hadhihi ummi' (this is my mother) â 'ummi' from 'umm' + 'i'. In a market in Egypt, a vendor might say 'hadha kitaabak' (this is your book) to a male customer. To form the possessive, you drop the final vowel of the noun if it has one, then add the suffix. For example, 'bayt' (house) + 'i' = 'bayti' (my house). 'sayyaara' (car) + 'i' = 'sayyaarati' (my car) â note the 't' reappears. For plural nouns, the suffix is added after the plural ending. For example, 'kutub' (books) + 'i' = 'kutubi' (my books). Practice by making sentences about your belongings: 'hadha qalami' (this is my pen), 'hadhihi sayyaarati' (this is my car). In African contexts, you might talk about your family: 'abi' (my father), 'ummi' (my mother), 'akhÄ«' (my brother), 'ukhtÄ«' (my sister). In business, 'sharikati' (my company), 'mashru'i' (my project). Listen to native speakers and note how they attach pronouns. In the Quran, 'rabbÄ«' (my Lord) and 'rabbuka' (your Lord) are common. To master, write sentences using all suffixes. Use a table to memorize: singular and plural, masculine and feminine. For example, 'kitaabÄ«' (my book), 'kitaabunÄ' (our book). Then practice with verbs as well, but for now, focus on nouns. In many African madrasas, students memorize these suffixes early. So, dedicate time to drills. Use apps like 'Arabic Unlocked' or 'Madinah Arabic' for practice. With repetition, you will internalize the patterns and speak more fluently.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Arabic Nouns, Gender, and Definite Articles for African Agribusiness

This Practical Reference lesson consolidates the six core lessons of the module â Masculine and Feminine Nouns, The Definite Article 'Al-' and Sun/Moon Letters, Indefinite Nouns and Tanwin, Singular, Dual, and Plural Forms, Demonstratives, and Possessive/Attached Pronouns â into one working desk reference. The goal is business-first: you should be able to read a supplier invoice, draft a short WhatsApp message to a Gulf or North African buyer, label a consignment, or negotiate a price in Arabic without pausing to re-derive the grammar. Arabic is the official language of 25+ countries and a working trade language across the Sahel, the Maghreb, Egypt, Sudan, and the Gulf â the same corridors that absorb African sesame, hibiscus, cocoa, coffee, livestock, and gum arabic. Getting the noun right is not academic; it is the difference between "one tonne" and "two tonnes," or between "the shipment" and "a shipment."

1. Gender: Masculine and Feminine Nouns

Arabic marks gender on nearly every noun, adjective, and pronoun. For business writing, the practical rule is: most nouns are masculine by default, and the common marker of femininity is the tÄ' marbÅ«á¹­a (Ø©) at the end of the word. A smaller set of nouns is feminine without any marker â these are the ones that catch exporters out.

2. The Definite Article 'Al-' and Sun/Moon Letters

The article Ø§ÙÙ (al-) makes a noun definite â "the shipment," not "a shipment." Its pronunciation changes depending on the first letter of the noun. With moon letters, the l is pronounced clearly: al-qamá¸¥ (Ø§ÙÙÙØ­, "the wheat"). With sun letters, the l assimilates into the following letter, which doubles: ash-shams (Ø§ÙØ´ÙØ³, "the sun"), as-sukkar (Ø§ÙØ³ÙØ±, "the sugar").

For agribusiness, this matters because the article attaches to product names, ports, and documents. When you say al-baá¸¥riyya (Ø§ÙØ¨Ø­Ø±ÙØ©, "the navy" or "maritime"), you are using a moon letter. When you say ash-sharika (Ø§ÙØ´Ø±ÙØ©, "the company"), you are using a sun letter. Getting the assimilation right signals competence to a Gulf buyer and avoids confusion on a voice note.

3. Indefinite Nouns and TanwÄ«n

Indefinite nouns take tanwÄ«n â the doubled short vowel at the end of the word, written as ÙÙ (nominative), ÙÙ (accusative), or ÙÙ (genitive). In spoken business Arabic, the final -n is often dropped, but in contracts and written correspondence it is essential. Shaá¸¥natun (Ø´ÙØ­ÙÙÙØ©Ù) = "a shipment"; shaá¸¥natun min al-qahwa (Ø´ÙØ­ÙÙÙØ©Ù ÙÙÙÙ Ø§ÙÙÙÙÙÙÙÙØ©) = "a shipment of coffee."

Practical rule: if you are quoting a new, unspecified quantity â "we can supply a container of sesame" â use tanwÄ«n. If you are referring to the specific consignment the buyer ordered â "the container of sesame is ready" â use al-.

4. Singular, Dual, and Plural Forms

Arabic has a dual form that English lacks. This is not a curiosity â it is commercially useful. á¹¬unn (Ø·ÙÙÙ) = one tonne; á¹­unnÄn (Ø·ÙÙÙÙØ§Ù) = two tonnes; aá¹­nÄn (Ø£ÙØ·ÙÙÙØ§Ù) = three or more tonnes. When a buyer in Cairo asks for á¹­unnÄn, they mean exactly two. Misreading the dual as a plural can double or halve a delivery.

Plurals come in two families: sound plurals (add ÙÙÙ / ÙÙÙ for masculine, ÙØ§Øª for feminine) and broken plurals (the internal vowel pattern changes). Agricultural nouns are heavily broken-plural: kÄ«s (ÙÙÙØ³, sack) â akyÄs (Ø£ÙÙÙÙÙØ§Ø³); á¹£undÅ«q (ØµÙÙÙØ¯ÙÙÙ, box) â á¹£anÄdÄ«q (ØµÙÙÙØ§Ø¯ÙÙÙ). Learn the plural with the singular from day one.

5. Demonstratives: This, That, These, Those

Demonstratives agree with the noun in gender and number:

  • Ø°ÙÙÙÙÙ (dhÄlika) â that (masc. sing.) â Ø°ÙÙÙÙÙ Ø§ÙØ³ÙÙØ¹ÙØ± (that price)
  • ØªÙÙÙÙÙ (tilka) â that (fem. sing.) â ØªÙÙÙÙÙ Ø§ÙÙÙÙØ²ÙØ±ÙØ¹ÙØ© (that farm)
  • ÙÙØ¤ÙÙÙØ§Ø¡Ù (hÄ'ulÄ'i) â these (plural) â ÙÙØ¤ÙÙÙØ§Ø¡Ù Ø§ÙÙÙÙÙÙØ±ÙÙØ¯ÙÙÙÙ (these suppliers)
  • Ø£ÙÙÙÙØ¦ÙÙÙ (ulÄ'ika) â those (plural) â Ø£ÙÙÙÙØ¦ÙÙÙ Ø§ÙÙØ¨ÙØ¶ÙØ§Ø¦ÙØ¹ (those goods)

In a WhatsApp negotiation, "this price" (ÙÙØ°ÙØ§ Ø§ÙØ³ÙÙØ¹ÙØ±) versus "that price" (Ø°ÙÙÙÙÙ Ø§ÙØ³ÙÙØ¹ÙØ±) can carry the difference between accepting the current quote and rejecting a previous one. Precision here is commercial, not cosmetic.

6. Possessive Pronouns and Attached Pronouns

Arabic expresses possession with suffixes attached to the noun, not with a separate word. The noun takes the suffix directly:

  • ÙÙÙ (-Ä«) â my â Ø´ÙØ±ÙÙÙØªÙÙ (my company)
  • ÙÙÙ (-ka) â your (masc.) â ÙÙØ²ÙØ±ÙØ¹ÙØªÙÙÙ (your farm)
  • ÙÙÙ (-ki) â your (fem.) â ÙÙØ²ÙØ±ÙØ¹ÙØªÙÙÙ (your farm)
  • ÙÙÙ (-hu) â his â ÙÙØ­ÙØµÙÙÙÙÙÙ (his crop)
  • ÙÙÙØ§ (-hÄ) â her â Ø´ÙØ±ÙÙÙØªÙÙÙØ§ (her company)
  • ÙÙÙØ§ (-nÄ) â our â ÙÙÙÙØ±ÙÙØ¯ÙÙÙØ§ (our supplier)
  • ÙÙÙÙÙ (-kum) â your (pl.) â Ø·ÙÙÙØ¨ÙÙÙÙÙ (your order)
  • ÙÙÙÙÙ (-hum) â their â Ø£ÙØ³ÙØ¹ÙØ§Ø±ÙÙÙÙÙ (their prices)

Because these suffixes attach to the noun, the noun loses its final tanwÄ«n: shaá¸¥natun becomes shaá¸¥natÄ« ("my shipment"). This is a common error in beginner business Arabic â writing Ø´ÙØ­ÙÙÙØ©Ù ÙÙÙ instead of the natural Ø´ÙØ­ÙÙÙØªÙÙ.

â  Safety Warning â Do Not Rely on Machine Translation for Contracts

Arabic noun forms carry legal weight. The dual versus plural distinction, the definite article, and attached pronouns can change quantities, ownership, and liability in a sales contract or letter of credit. Never sign, issue, or accept an Arabic-language contract, bill of lading, or phytosanitary certificate based solely on a machine translation or a quick phone translation. A misplaced tanwÄ«n or a misread dual can convert "two containers" into "containers" and expose your agribusiness to a delivery dispute, a rejected LC, or a customs penalty. Always have a qualified human translator or a bilingual trade lawyer review binding Arabic documents before signature.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Gender first. Check whether the noun ends in Ø© (feminine) before choosing adjectives, demonstratives, and pronouns.
  2. Definite or indefinite? Use Ø§ÙÙ for a specific, agreed consignment; use tanwÄ«n (ÙÙ ÙÙ ÙÙ) for a new or unspecified one.
  3. Sun or moon? Assimilate the l of Ø§ÙÙ before sun letters (Ø´ Ø³ Ø° Ù Ù Ø± Øª Ø¯ Ø· Ø² Øµ Ø¶ Ø« Ø¸); pronounce it before moon letters.
  4. Count carefully. Dual (ÙØ§Ù) means exactly two; broken plurals mean three or more. Never treat a dual as a plural.
  5. Match demonstratives. ÙÙØ°ÙØ§ / Ø°ÙÙÙÙÙ for masculine, ÙÙØ°ÙÙÙ / ØªÙÙÙÙÙ for feminine, ÙÙØ¤ÙÙÙØ§Ø¡Ù / Ø£ÙÙÙÙØ¦ÙÙÙ for plurals.
  6. Attach possessives. Write Ø´ÙØ±ÙÙÙØªÙÙ, not Ø´ÙØ±ÙÙÙØ©Ù ÙÙÙ. Drop the tanwÄ«n when a possessive suffix is added.
  7. Verify quantities in writing. Repeat the number, unit, and noun in both Arabic and a second language on invoices and packing lists.
  8. Escalate binding documents. Route contracts, LCs, and certificates through a qualified human translator before signature.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • Arabic Reading Course â free structured lessons on the alphabet, sun/moon letters, and noun forms.
  • Madinah Arabic â free grammar modules covering gender, definiteness, dual, and plural, widely used by African self-learners.
  • FAOTERM â FAO Arabic Terminology Database â official multilingual terminology for agriculture, food, and trade, with Arabic equivalents.
  • WTO Accession and Trade Documentation â official trade-language references, including Arabic-language trade documents from Arab League members.
  • African Union â Arabic Language Resources â AU documents and terminology in Arabic, useful for pan-African trade correspondence.

Prepared for the RISE AFRICA Skills programme â Arabic Language, Module: Nouns, Gender, and Definite Articles. This Practical Reference is a study aid and does not replace qualified legal or translation review of binding commercial documents.

quiz.q: Which of the following nouns is feminine?
quiz.explanation: Sayyaara ends with the feminine marker Ø©, making it feminine.

quiz.q: What is the definite article in Arabic?
quiz.explanation: Al- is the definite article, meaning 'the'.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sun letter?
quiz.explanation: Sh is a sun letter, so the 'l' in 'al-' is assimilated.

quiz.q: How do you pronounce 'al-shams' (the sun) correctly?
quiz.explanation: Sh is a sun letter, so the 'l' is not pronounced and the 'sh' is doubled.

quiz.q: What is the indefinite form of 'kitaab' (book) in the nominative?
quiz.explanation: Tanwin 'un' is added for indefinite nominative.

quiz.q: Which tanwin is used for indefinite genitive?
quiz.explanation: The kasratÄn (-in) is used for genitive indefinite nouns.

quiz.q: What is the dual form of 'walad' (boy) in the nominative?
quiz.explanation: The dual nominative adds 'aani' to the singular.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'kitaab' (book)?
quiz.explanation: Kutub is a broken plural of kitaab.

quiz.q: Which demonstrative means 'this' for a feminine singular noun?
quiz.explanation: Hadhihi is used for feminine singular near objects.

quiz.q: How do you say 'that is a house' (masculine singular)?
quiz.explanation: Dhaalika is the masculine singular far demonstrative.

quiz.q: What is the possessive suffix for 'my'?
quiz.explanation: The suffix -i indicates 'my' when attached to a noun.

quiz.q: How do you say 'your book' to a male?
quiz.explanation: The suffix -ka is used for masculine 'your'.

quiz.q: Which of these nouns is masculine?
quiz.explanation: Baab does not have the feminine ending and is masculine.

quiz.q: What is the correct pronunciation of 'al-qamar' (the moon)?
quiz.explanation: Q is a moon letter, so the 'l' is pronounced.

quiz.explanation: The fatá¸¥atÄn (-an) is used for accusative indefinite nouns.

quiz.q: What is the dual form of 'bint' (girl) in the accusative?
quiz.explanation: The dual accusative adds 'ayni' to the singular.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'mu'allim' (teacher) using sound masculine plural?
quiz.explanation: Sound masculine plural nominative adds 'uuna'.

quiz.q: Which demonstrative means 'these' for plural nouns?
quiz.explanation: Haa'ulaa'i is used for near plural demonstrative.

quiz.q: How do you say 'those are students' (masculine plural)?
quiz.explanation: Ulaa'ika is the far plural demonstrative.

quiz.q: What is the possessive suffix for 'her'?
quiz.explanation: The suffix -ha indicates 'her'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'our house'?
quiz.explanation: The suffix -na indicates 'our'.

quiz.q: Which of these is a moon letter?
quiz.explanation: B is a moon letter, so 'al-' is pronounced fully.

quiz.q: What is the indefinite form of 'bayt' (house) in the genitive?
quiz.explanation: Tanwin 'in' is added for indefinite genitive.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'bint' (girl)?
quiz.explanation: Banaat is the broken plural of bint.

quiz.q: Which demonstrative means 'that' for a feminine singular noun?
quiz.explanation: Tilka is the feminine singular far demonstrative.

quiz.q: How do you say 'my pen'?
quiz.explanation: The suffix -i indicates 'my' on qalam.

quiz.q: Which of these nouns is feminine by nature, not by ending?
quiz.explanation: Umm (mother) is feminine without the Ø© ending.

quiz.q: What is the correct pronunciation of 'al-nil' (the Nile)?
quiz.explanation: N is a sun letter, so the 'l' is assimilated, making it 'an-nil'.

quiz.q: What is the dual form of 'sayyaara' (car) in the nominative?
quiz.explanation: The dual nominative adds 'aani' to the singular, with the feminine 't' reappearing.

quiz.explanation: The suffix -ki is used for feminine 'your'.
